newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Apr 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Apr 4.

text.p: A summit meeting to discuss a kiwifruit grower's right to choose how and where he disposes of his fruit was written into the coalition agreement at the insistence of NZ First. That was back in December. It now seems likely that deregulation -- the issue which for years has ripped apart the kiwifruit industry -- is off-limits if, and when, the summit is ever convened. Tentatively scheduled for 22 July, the date and the agenda have yet to be set. Page 1.

The government will now let the public in on its secret superannuation talks. On Thursday afternoon -- apparently at the request of its design team -- it undertook to "invite comment on the design of the compulsory superannuation option." The statement, from the office of the Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters, said advertisements will be placed in daily papers tomorrow and next Wednesday inviting submissions from interested parties. The deadline for submissions is 1 May. Page 1.

Foreign Affairs and Treasury officials are negotiating an international treaty to restrict government controls on flows of investment capital. The Overseas Investment Commission is also involved in shaping New Zealand's position on the pact. They are negotiating consistent with the government's opening economy policy and the country's need for inflows of capital from overseas. Drafts of the treaty -- known as the Multilateral Agreement on Investment -- are not being made public. Page 2.

Despite telecommunications industry deregulation, New Zealand has some of the highest toll and business line telephone charges in the OECD. So says a recent survey of 12 OECD countries conducted by NUS International Pty Ltd, an Australian energy and telecommunications cost analyst. Both Telecom and Clear are shown to have the highest international toll charges -- after being ranked fourth five years ago. They also have the third highest rates for national toll calls and charge the second most expensive rates for business line rental. Page 3.

The newly-demutualised Colonial Ltd on Thursday launched its prospectus, signalling the closing stages of a five-year plan. That plan was to transform the company from a traditional mutual life office into a listed international financial services group. Central to that strategy ws demutualisation and expansion outside life insurance. Colonial achieved the former with its December 1994 purchase of the State Bank of NSW (now renamed Colonial State Bank) for A$576 million. Last November's policyholder vote gave demutualisation the green light. Page 3.

The Employers Federation this week welcomed a Court of Appeal decision which, it says, significantly reinforces the sanctity of contract law on employment-related issues. Deputy chief executive Anne Knowles says the ruling in Auckland College of Education v Hagg is "an indication that the Court of Appeal is clearly of the view that a contract is a contract is a contract." Page 4.

The Fisheries Ministry has rejected fishing industry calls for recreational fishermen to suffer the same cuts to their catch as those being imposed in commercial fishermen. Such constraints would not be legal or practical, lawyers acting for the ministry told the High Court in Wellington this week. The fishing industry and several Maori groups are seeking a judicial review of the ministry's decision to cut the commercial snapper catch in the waters off the Bay of Plenty, the Hauraki Gulf and Northland by 39 percent. Page 6.

People used to moan about the Post Office. They complained bitterly when its successor, New Zealand Post, closed 432 post offices in 1987. Today, a decade after New Zealand Post came into being, the critics are all but silent. The corporation not only provides a better service and returns a healthy dividend to the government but it has also made history as perhaps the world's only mail service to cut the standard rate of postage. page 6.

Speculation that Christchurch-based clothing company LWR Industries would be broken up was discounted by grouop managing director Terry Iggo this week after his return from the UK where it is understood the company has been seeking a joint-venture partner for its Canterbury International Group subsidiary. A decision on the joint venture was expected in mid-May. En route Iggo visited Hong Kong where LWR has expanded its purchasing office as it increases its volume of imports to counter competition from imports. Page 10.

DB's managing director Brian Blake says while competitor Lion appears to be preparing the market for a softer upcoming profit result, his company is continuing to increase its market share of the declining beer market. Blake said that from mid-1995 his company had increased its market share of beer sales every month. Recent advertising and promotional campaings using a Clydesdale team of horses had proved particularly effective for DB Draught, he said. Page 11.

Top Top's excess manufacturing capacity, particularly in its Christchurch factory, is likely to be used by its new owners for additional export products to Australia and Japan. Gram Laitt, the managing director Western Australia-based Peteers & Brownes Foods, which has bought Tip Top from H J Heinz for about $200 millin, dismissed fears of redundancies and contraction and said the intention was quite the opposite. Page 11.
